lines.note: Izzuremo is glossed as all, then as in any case or finally. It is the entry anticipated by the preceding page's catchword; the final ca- continues below.
The opening ſo completes caſo, followed by finalmente. The scan places this continuation inward from the headword margin.
Izzureno is another form glossed as all. It remains an independent headword rather than being merged with Izzuremo.
Izzutçu means the mouth or curb of a well, matching bocal do poço. This is the last izz- entry before the consonantal-I section.

runs.text: Retribuição: ſempre ſe vſa com algũa cõ

lines.note: IA denotes requital or recompense and is said to occur in compounds. The initial I spans two physical lines and was lost by OCR; Retribuição and its colon are recovered from the damaged Portuguese word.
Poſição completes composição, explaining the compound-only usage. Iaxite illustrates requiting or repaying, directly matched by Retribuindo.
Fôja ſuru is a second example of rendering recompense. The Portuguese Retribuir is recoverable despite abrasion of its early letters; no word space is inserted inside it.
This separate Ia means snake or serpent. It is consonantal I, read with a j-like value, not the OCR long s.
Another Ia means evil or wrong, explained by Yocoxima. The example begins turning away from evil; its verb continues on the next row.
The opening yexi completes firugayexi, followed by the separately printed xǒni qiſu, returning to what is right. The Portuguese begins correcting vices; its conjunction leads into the next line.
Darſe means to devote oneself, completing the explanation as turning to virtue and justice. The apparent t in the draft is a long s; Xix. is the citation label and remains roman.

Iaacu means perverse or evil, explained by Yocoxima acu. Enlargement confirms two a sorts, the first partly joined to the initial I; there is no legible stop after the headword, so none is supplied. The post-reading NINJAL checkpoint prompted this reinspection (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima, assisted by Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); its normalized punctuation is not copied.
Ou deſordenada adds disorderly to the preceding characterization of evil. It belongs to Iaacu, not to the next snake-related entry.
Iabi is a snake’s tail, unpacked as Iano vo. The middle consonant of Iano is n rather than the OCR u; the Portuguese Rabo de ſerpente confirms the genitive construction.

runs.text: Cestos como canaſtras com pedras den-

lines.note: Iacago denotes stone-filled basket structures. The Portuguese starts describing baskets like large hampers with stones inside; den- continues as dentro below.

runs.text: tro, q̃ poem ao longo dos rios, ou pera ter mão

lines.note: The baskets are placed along rivers, with ter mão beginning the explanation of holding the earth in place. The nasal abbreviation q̃ is retained rather than expanded to que.

runs.text: na terra, que não ſe desfaça, ou pera repre-

lines.note: This line explains preventing the earth from coming apart, then begins the alternative purpose of damming water. Repre- must be joined semantically with ſar on the following physical row.
The fragment ſar completes repreſar: retaining or damming the water. Agoa is the printed historical spelling, not an error to modernize to água.

Iacǒ first denotes an animal that yields musk; the next sense is the musk itself. The scan supports almiſcre, with c after the long s rather than the OCR e, and a consonantal initial I in the headword.
This is the second Iacǒ sense: the musk itself. Almiſcre matches the preceding line; the draft’s alinſere loses the m and mistakes c for e.
Iacǒguan is identified simply as a medicine. The entry does not specify its ingredients here, so the gloss is not expanded into a modern pharmaceutical identification.
Iacot is snake bone, explained by Iano fone. The n of Iano is faint but fits the surviving shape and the genitive phrase; final t and the printed Oßo ligature are preserved.
The snake bone is described as serving medicinally. The damaged consonant in mezinha is n, consistent with the same word clearly printed two rows earlier.
Iacqet is explained by Ybara as a thorny tree so called. The scan gives Aruore and aßi rather than the OCR Atuore and aße; the joined deſpinhos and the ß ligature remain diplomatic.
This Iacu means weak or weakness, as Youaxi and the Portuguese mutually confirm. The initial is consonantal I, not long s.
A homographic Iacu denotes quietness, explained by Xizzuca nari. It is a separate sense from weakness and retains the printed division of Xizzuca nari.
Iacufai describes someone young, expanded as Vacaqi tomogara. The Portuguese begins a young man or someone of little age, continuing on the following row.

runs.text: pouca idade. ¶ Item, Serue pera ſe humi-

lines.note: After completing the literal youth sense, the paragraph adds a self-humbling use. Humi- is divided before lhar across the next line.

runs.text: lhar moſtrandoſe de pouco ſaber, & idade po

lines.note: The humble use presents the speaker as having little knowledge and age. The terminal po belongs to posto on the next row; no unprinted hyphen is supplied.
The speaker may use Iacufai humbly despite actually being of considerable age. The example Iacufaina cotouo starts on this row, with its verb below.

runs.text: Dizer couſas de homem de pouca idade,

lines.note: Yǔ completes the example: saying things characteristic of a young or inexperienced person. The long-vowel mark is kept as printed rather than replaced by modern spelling.
Ou pouco ſaber extends the example to speech betraying little knowledge. This short continuation completes Iacufai before a new quietness-related entry.
Iacujacuto is an adverb meaning quietly or peacefully. The abbreviation is Adu., not Alu.; ſoſegadamẽ continues with te on the next physical row.

Te completes ſoſegadamente, followed by the Buddhist-usage label Bup. The isolated parenthesis and quietação occupy the far right of this physical row but complete the following entry’s Paz, ou; their displaced placement is retained rather than moving them into semantic reading order.
Iacujǒ is explained with Xizzucani and xizzuca nari as peace or quietness. Its final quietação is physically displaced to the preceding row’s right end and is encoded there.
Iacujǔ combines the ideas of weakness and softness, explained by Youaxi and yauaraca. The scan supports c in yauaraca, not the draft’s t; the initial I and unhyphenated cou are retained.
The opening ſa completes couſa, yielding weakness or something weak. It is a continuation of Iacujǔ, not an independent definition.
Iacumacu is a quiet state or quietness, explained by Xizzucana coto. The Portuguese alternative introduced by ou continues below.

Quietação completes the general definition and is printed with i, omitted in the draft. Iacumacu muninjǒ introduces a more specific quiet condition, whose Portuguese explanation starts with the divided Quie-.

runs.text: tação, & repouſo ſem ouuir vozes, ou eſtron

lines.note: The compound means quiet and repose without hearing voices or human noise. The scan supports ouuir, not the OCR ouair; eſtron continues into eſtrondo on the next row without a supplied hyphen.
Do completes eſtrondo, followed by de gente: the noise of people. The physical division is preserved even though the word is interpreted continuously.

Iacumet concerns cessation or extinction, explained by the following Japanese phrase. The faint initial I is retained, and the scan shows two long-s sorts in meſſu; Monono begins the explanatory alternative completed below.
Meſsuru completes Monono meſsuru, glossed as ending or dying. The final Iacumet begins the next example without the spurious stop supplied by OCR; its object particle is on the following row.

This completes Iacumet uo tonǒ, likewise glossed as ending or dying and marked for Buddhist usage. The source’s tonǒ is retained, and the terminal stop belongs with roman Bup., not an isolated italic run.
The 9 is widely spaced from 13; together they constitute the printed page number, separate from the running header.
Iacunan is a young man, made explicit by Vacai votoco and Mancebo. The terminal S. is a usage label, not part of the Japanese phrase.
Iacunen here denotes youth in years, expanded as Vacai toxi. This age sense is distinct from the homograph for quietness a few rows below.
Imada jacunenni gozaru illustrates still being young. The example uses lowercase j within the sentence, unlike the consonantal capital I of the headword; both spellings are retained.
Pouca idade completes the translation of still being of little age. It is the short continuation of the preceding Japanese example.
This second Iacunen means quietness, with Xizzucana coto as its explanatory phrase. It is not merged with the preceding age-related Iacunen.
Iacuro and the alternative zacuro denote a pomegranate or its tree. The initial I is restored; the printed Romaã and romeira are retained instead of modern Portuguese spellings.
Iacurono qi specifies the pomegranate tree rather than the fruit. The Japanese qi and Portuguese Romeira agree.
Iacurozaca describes a cock’s comb likened to a pomegranate. The Portuguese is Criſta, with a dotted i and long-s/t sequence, not the draft’s Crũba.
Iadǒ is the way of evil, expanded as Yocoximano michi. The Portuguese mal continues unhyphenated into maldade on the next physical row.
After completing maldade, the entry gives Iadǒuo voconǒ, practising evil. Cometer introduces the Portuguese translation continued below.
The translation of Iadǒuo voconǒ is to commit evil acts or sins. The Portuguese uses pecados with a single c here, unlike peccado later on the page.
Iafeqi is a bad habit, explained by Yocoximano cuxe. The Portuguese plural cuſtumes introduces the corresponding habits or customs.
The example Iafeqiuo aratamuru means reforming bad habits. The final E- begins Emendar, and its printed hyphen remains on this row.
Mendar completes Emendar: to correct bad habits. Maos is retained as printed rather than modernized to maus.
Iafi is snake skin, expanded as Iano caua. Both the genitive phrase and Pelle de ſerpente support this reading.
Iafô denotes an evil or perverse law or teaching, with Yocoximana nori and Mafô as explanations. The initial I is restored while the printed circumflexes and Ley are preserved.
Ou peruerſa completes the description of the law or teaching. This belongs to Iafô, not to the following wind entry.

Iafǔ denotes a harmful, pestilential wind. Enlargement shows the abraded but surviving bowl and cross-stroke of e after caj, supporting caje; the letter is restored rather than accepting the OCR omission.
Ro completes peſtifero and vento supplies the noun wind. The interrupted Portuguese adjective follows its original physical line division.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de inchaço, ou poſtema

lines.note: Iaganchǒ is described as a kind of swelling or abscess. The next row specifies its bodily location; no modern diagnosis is imposed on the historical term.

runs.text: que nace nas mãos, & nos pees.

lines.note: The swelling or abscess is said to arise on the hands and feet. The printed nace and pees are historical forms and are not modernized.
Iago means an evil or perverse utterance, explained by Yocoximano go. The initial is I, not the OCR long s; the Portuguese noun follows below.
Sentença completes the definition as a bad or perverse statement. The long initial ſ belongs to Portuguese, unlike the restored I of the Japanese headword above.
Iaguen is explained by Yocoxima manaco as indecent or improper eyes or looks. The Portuguese desho- continues onto the next physical row.
Nestos completes deshonestos, followed by the source’s usage label S. The label is kept separate in interpretation from the Portuguese adjective.
Iagui denotes falsity or deceit, expanded with Yocoxima and itçuuaru. The source’s doubled-u sequence in itçuuaru is retained, not simplified.
Mentira supplies the alternative gloss lie. It is the final continuation of Iagui before the distinct Iaguiǒ entry.
Iaguiǒ means evil deeds, explained by Yocoximano voconai. The accented Màs is retained as printed rather than regularized.
Iajei denotes a snake’s sloughed skin, metaphorically expanded as Cuchinauano qinu. The faint initial I is visible and restored; q̃ is kept as the printed abbreviation.
The skin is that which snakes leave behind or shed. Deſpem is the source’s verb form and is preserved without modernization.
Iaji denotes an evil or disorderly matter, explained by Yocoximano coto. The damaged mark over mã is retained from the aligned reading rather than regularized to another accent.
Ordenada completes deſordenada, describing something disordered. The division after deſ- is kept on its original row.

runs.text: Cami, ou diabo mao, & prejudicial, ou que

lines.note: Iajin is an evil or harmful spirit: the Portuguese embeds the Japanese Cami before comparing it to a devil. The scan reads diabo mao and prejudicial; OCR had damaged diabo, misread the final vowel of mao, and dropped the l of prejudicial.
The final clause says that the spirit always does harm. This completes the historical characterization in the preceding gloss, rather than making a claim about religious belief.
Iain is glossed as lust or sensuality, and Iainuo begins an example. Its spelling differs from the preceding Iajin and is not regularized to match it.
Vocaſu completes the example, translated as committing the sin of lust. The doubled cc in peccado is visibly printed here and differs from the earlier pecados.
Iama first denotes a devil, with Yocoxima tengu as explanation. The following Item introduces the extended sense of obstruction or interference.

runs.text: Eſtoruo que ſe faz a alguem em algũa ocupa-

lines.note: The second sense is an obstacle imposed on someone engaged in an activity. Eſtoruo and ocupa- retain their historical spelling and line-ending division.
After completing ocupação, the example describes obstructing study: Gacumonno jamauo ſuru, with an alternative beginning ja-. The lowercase j forms are kept as printed.
Mani completes jamani naru, the alternative expression for being an impediment. The Portuguese begins to hinder someone in their study and continues below.
Estudo completes the translation of hindering someone’s studies. The short continuation belongs to the Iama example, not to Iaman below.
Iaman is arrogance or pride, explained with Yocoximanaru manqi. The abraded initial I is restored; Soberba is the Portuguese gloss rather than a label.
Iamǒ here denotes evil desires, with Yocoximano nozomi as explanation. The entry that follows uses the same headword for a disturbed mental state, so both entries remain separate.
Iamǒuo toguru coto nacare is a prohibition against fulfilling evil desires. The Portuguese Não cũ begins the matching negative command; its nasal abbreviation remains unexpanded.
Pras completes cũpras, yielding do not fulfil evil desires. The line division and the source’s maos are preserved.
This Iamǒ describes a mind disordered by evil desires, expanded as Yocoximani midarinari. The Portuguese per continues without a printed hyphen into perturbado below.

Turbado completes perturbado. The next Japanese example starts Iamǒuo ca- and continues beyond this page; the separate catchword taximu- anticipates that continuation and is not appended to the body row.
This anticipates the continuation of body-final ca- on the next page; it is ordinary roman catchword text, not part of the signature.
